question: King Ahab and Queen Jezebel had filled Israel with Baal worship. The prophet Elijah challenged 450 prophets of Baal to a contest on Mount Carmel: each side would build an altar, lay a bull on the wood, and call on their god to light the fire. The prophets of Baal danced and cut themselves all day; nothing happened. Elijah then drenched his altar with twelve jars of water until a trench around it overflowed. He prayed once. What happened?
answer: Fire fell from heaven and consumed the bull, wood, stones, and water
choices: Fire fell from heaven and consumed the bull, wood, stones, and water
A thick cloud rose from the sea and covered the altar in mist
The bull rose to its feet and walked away unharmed by the priests
Lightning split the altar in two without burning the offering
context: 1 Kings 18. Elijah then ordered the 450 prophets of Baal seized and killed at the brook Kishon. Jezebel swore to have him dead within a day; Elijah fled into the wilderness, where God fed him by ravens at the brook Cherith. The twelve jars echoed the twelve tribes of Israel - Elijah was forcing a national choice.

question: After his victory on Mount Carmel, the prophet Elijah fled Queen Jezebel's death threat into the wilderness, traveled forty days to Mount Horeb, and hid in a cave. God told him to come out and stand on the mountain. A great wind tore the rocks; God was not in the wind. Then an earthquake; God was not in it. Then a fire; God was not in it. After the fire came something Elijah recognized at once, covering his face with his cloak. What came after the fire?
answer: A still small voice (a gentle whisper)
choices: A still small voice (a gentle whisper)
A blinding light brighter than the noon sun
A great voice like the roar of many waters
A clap of thunder that shook the mountain
context: 1 Kings 19:11-13. The Hebrew phrase 'qol demamah daqqah' literally means 'a sound of thin silence' - God speaks here in the smallest possible voice, the opposite of the storm-god theophany the audience would have expected. Elijah was sent back with three commissions: anoint Hazael king of Aram, Jehu king of Israel, and Elisha as his own successor.

question: When the Assyrian king Sennacherib marched on Jerusalem in 701 BC, King Hezekiah of Judah prepared the city for siege. Hezekiah's stonecutters dug an S-shaped tunnel 1,750 feet through limestone to secure the water supply, two teams meeting in the middle. The tunnel still carries water today. When Sennacherib's commander mocked Hezekiah's God in Hebrew loud enough for the defenders to hear, what destroyed the Assyrian army that night?
answer: An angel struck down 185,000 men in the camp before dawn
choices: An angel struck down 185,000 men in the camp before dawn
An Egyptian raid surprised the camp from the southern desert
A flash flood swept the camp into the Kidron valley below
Sennacherib's own bodyguard turned against him in the night
context: 2 Kings 18-19 and Isaiah 36-37. The Greek historian Herodotus preserves an Egyptian tradition that field mice gnawed Assyrian bowstrings overnight - possibly a memory of a rodent-borne plague. Sennacherib withdrew to Nineveh and was later assassinated by his own sons. Hezekiah's tunnel was rediscovered by a swimming boy in 1838 and the Siloam inscription describing the dig was found inside.

question: Nehemiah was cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I when he heard that the walls of Jerusalem still lay in ruins from Babylonian destruction 140 years earlier. He wept, fasted, and asked the king for leave and timber. He arrived in Jerusalem secretly, inspected the broken walls at night by donkey, and rallied the people to rebuild. Hostile neighbors led by Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite mocked and threatened. Nehemiah armed the workmen so each could build with one hand while doing what with the other?
answer: Held a weapon (sword or spear) in the other
choices: Held a weapon (sword or spear) in the other
Carried a torch to light the work after dark
Held a water-jar to wet the mortar quickly
Held a horn ready to sound the alarm
context: Nehemiah 4. The walls were completed in just 52 days. Nehemiah and Ezra together led a renewal of Jerusalem after the exile - Ezra reading the Law aloud at the Water Gate while the people wept, and Nehemiah governing the rebuilt city. Their books, Ezra-Nehemiah, are the last narrative books of the Hebrew Bible chronologically.

question: On the night before his last battle against the Philistines, King Saul of Israel was terrified - Samuel was long dead, God no longer answered his prayers, the Philistine army was massed at Gilboa. Though Saul himself had outlawed mediums on pain of death, he disguised himself and traveled to the village of Endor to consult a woman who could call up the dead. She raised a spirit at his request. The medium screamed when she recognized whom she had summoned. Who came up?
answer: The prophet Samuel, who prophesied Saul's death the next day
choices: The prophet Samuel, who prophesied Saul's death the next day
Saul's father Kish, weeping over his son's failure
Saul's own ancestor Benjamin, blessing the line of kings
The patriarch Abraham, demanding repentance from Saul
context: 1 Samuel 28. Samuel announced: 'Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.' Saul collapsed full-length on the ground in terror. The next day at Mount Gilboa the Philistines killed Saul's three sons (including Jonathan, David's friend). Saul, wounded by arrows, fell on his own sword to avoid capture. His head was cut off and his body nailed to the wall of Beth-shan.

question: King David, idle in Jerusalem one spring while his army was at war, saw a beautiful woman bathing on a rooftop. He learned she was Bathsheba, wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his own loyal soldiers fighting at the front. David sent for her, slept with her, and got her pregnant. To cover the affair he had Uriah placed in the heaviest fighting and abandoned. Uriah died. The prophet Nathan came to David with a story about a rich man who stole a poor neighbor's beloved lamb for a guest's dinner. David flew into a rage and demanded the rich man's death. What did Nathan reply?
answer: You are that man, David
choices: You are that man, David
God has heard the lamb cry out
Such a man dies by his own decree
Beware lest your kingdom be torn from you
context: 2 Samuel 11-12. David collapsed and wrote what became Psalm 51 ('Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love...'). The first child of the union died; the second, born after his repentance, was Solomon. Nathan also prophesied that 'the sword would never depart' from David's house - Absalom's later revolt and the killing of David's son Amnon by his brother both fulfilled it.

question: Job was a wealthy righteous man in the land of Uz with seven sons, three daughters, 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 donkeys. In a single day four messengers arrived: Sabean raiders had taken the oxen; lightning had killed the sheep; Chaldeans had taken the camels; a great wind had collapsed the house on his ten children. Job tore his robe, shaved his head, fell to the ground - and worshipped. What did he say?
answer: The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord
choices: The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord
Let me hide my face from God and never see his light again
Curse the day I was born, and let darkness claim it
Who is the Lord that he should test his faithful servant so
context: Job 1:21. The Book of Job is one of the oldest and longest meditations on innocent suffering in world literature. After thirty-seven chapters of debate with his friends (Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar) over WHY he suffers, God speaks from the whirlwind without ever answering the question - only revealing the wildness of creation (Behemoth, Leviathan). Job is restored doubly: 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, ten more children, lives 140 more years.

question: King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) of Persia held a 180-day banquet for his nobles, then a seven-day feast at the palace gardens of Susa with wine flowing freely. On the seventh day, with the king's heart 'merry with wine,' he sent eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti before the assembled men so they could see her beauty. Vashti refused. The king's anger burned. His advisor Memucan warned: if her defiance went unpunished, every wife in Persia would copy her. What did Memucan recommend?
answer: Depose Vashti and give her royal position to another woman
choices: Depose Vashti and give her royal position to another woman
Send her home to her family in chains for three years
Force her to appear at the next banquet under guard
Have her quietly poisoned in her own chambers that night
context: Esther 1. The king issued a decree that every man should be master in his own house - read in Hebrew, Persian, and every language of the empire. A search of all the beautiful young virgins of the empire followed; Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, was eventually chosen as the new queen. The book of Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible that does not name God.

question: Haman, grand vizier of Persia, had built a 75-foot gallows on which to hang Esther's cousin Mordecai. That night the king could not sleep. The chronicles were read aloud, reminding him that Mordecai had exposed a plot but never been rewarded. The king summoned Haman, just arrived to ask leave to hang Mordecai. The king asked: 'What should be done for the man the king wishes to honor?' Haman, sure the king meant himself, suggested royal robes and a parade. The king ordered him to do exactly that. For whom?
answer: Mordecai the Jew, led through Susa by Haman himself
choices: Mordecai the Jew, led through Susa by Haman himself
The king's own son, the crown prince of Persia
The captain of the royal guard who saved his life
Haman himself, to honor his long and loyal service
context: Esther 6. Haman was forced to dress Mordecai in royal robes, mount him on the king's own horse, and lead him through the streets of Susa proclaiming: 'Thus shall be done to the man the king wishes to honor.' Haman went home humiliated; his wife and friends warned him this was the beginning of his fall. He was summoned to Esther's second banquet that same evening, where she named him as the architect of the planned genocide of the Jews. Haman was hanged on his own gallows that night.

question: In the Roman colony of Philippi, the apostle Paul cast a fortune-telling spirit out of a slave girl, and her angry owners dragged Paul and Silas before the magistrates. They were beaten with rods, locked in the inner prison, feet in wooden stocks. About midnight as they prayed and sang hymns aloud, a violent earthquake shook the jail. The doors flew open and every prisoner's chains fell off. The terrified jailer drew his sword to kill himself rather than face execution for their escape. What did Paul shout?
answer: Do not harm yourself, for we are all still here
choices: Do not harm yourself, for we are all still here
Stand up and walk out before the soldiers come
Run and tell the magistrate the gods have spoken
Throw down your sword, the city is judged tonight
context: Acts 16. The jailer fell trembling at their feet, asked what he must do to be saved, took them home, washed their wounds, and was baptized that night with all his household. The next day the magistrates ordered Paul and Silas quietly released - but Paul, a Roman citizen who had been beaten without trial, demanded a public apology. The magistrates came in person and escorted them out of the city.

question: After feeding the five thousand, Jesus sent the disciples ahead in their boat across the Sea of Galilee and went up the mountain alone to pray. Around three in the morning, with the wind churning the waves, the disciples were straining at the oars far from shore. They saw Jesus walking toward them on the water and cried out in terror, thinking it was a ghost. Jesus called: 'Take heart, it is I.' Peter answered: 'Lord, if it is you, command me to come.' Peter climbed out and walked - then noticed the wind and began to sink. What did Peter cry out?
answer: Lord, save me!
choices: Lord, save me!
The waters take me!
Forgive my doubt!
Hold out your hand!
context: Matthew 14:22-33. Jesus reached out, caught him, and said: 'You of little faith, why did you doubt?' When the two of them climbed into the boat, the wind died. The disciples worshipped him, saying: 'Truly you are the Son of God.' Peter walking on water is recorded only in Matthew (Mark and John tell the rest of the storm story but not this scene).

question: Traveling through Samaria around noon, Jesus stopped at Jacob's well in the village of Sychar while his disciples went into town for food. A Samaritan woman came alone to draw water (the unusual hour suggested she was avoiding the other village women). Jesus asked her for a drink. She was startled - Jews and Samaritans normally did not speak, and the request also crossed gender lines. He offered her 'living water' so she would never thirst again. When she asked for this water, what did Jesus tell her to do first?
answer: Go call your husband and come back
choices: Go call your husband and come back
Bring the elders of the village to me
Climb down into the well and bathe yourself
Bring an empty jar from your house to fill
context: John 4. The woman answered: 'I have no husband.' Jesus replied: 'You have had five husbands, and the man you are with now is not your husband.' She left her jar, ran to the town, and brought a crowd back - and many Samaritans believed because of her. The discussion of true worship ('neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth') with a Samaritan woman is one of the longest one-on-one conversations Jesus has in any Gospel.

question: On the evening of the first Easter, the disciples were gathered in a locked room in Jerusalem out of fear of the authorities. The risen Jesus appeared among them, showed his hands and his side, and breathed the Holy Spirit on them. But the disciple Thomas, called Didymus ('the twin'), was not there. When the others told him 'We have seen the Lord,' he refused to believe. Eight days later Jesus appeared again in the same room with Thomas present. What did Jesus tell Thomas to do?
answer: Put your finger here and your hand into my side
choices: Put your finger here and your hand into my side
Eat with me of the bread and the broiled fish
Walk with me down to the road to Emmaus
Wash my feet as you did before the supper
context: John 20:24-29. Thomas answered: 'My Lord and my God.' Jesus said: 'Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.' Tradition (the Acts of Thomas, c. 3rd century) holds that Thomas later carried the gospel to India and was martyred near Madras around 72 AD by being run through with spears. The St. Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to him.

question: On the night Jesus was arrested in Gethsemane, Peter followed at a distance to the courtyard of the high priest Caiaphas. He sat warming himself by a charcoal fire in the cold night air. A servant girl looked at him: 'You also were with Jesus the Galilean.' Peter denied it. A second girl spoke. He denied again with an oath. A third bystander said his Galilean accent gave him away. Peter denied a third time, swearing he did not know the man. What signal then made him remember Jesus's exact prediction?
answer: A rooster crowed in the courtyard
choices: A rooster crowed in the courtyard
A trumpet sounded from the temple wall
A donkey brayed near the stable gate
A guard struck a bronze gong for the watch
context: Mark 14:66-72 and parallels in Matthew 26, Luke 22, John 18. Jesus had predicted at the supper: 'Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.' Peter went out and wept bitterly. The first chapter of John's appendix (John 21) records the risen Jesus's threefold restoration of Peter at another charcoal fire on the shore of Galilee - three questions ('Do you love me?') to match the three denials.

question: Paul was being shipped under guard from Caesarea to Rome to stand trial before Caesar when a fierce northeaster called the Euroclydon drove the grain freighter off course for fourteen days. On the night the crew finally suspected land, soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners to stop any swimming away; the centurion refused for Paul's sake. The ship struck a reef at dawn near Malta; all 276 reached shore alive. The Maltese kindled a fire for the soaked survivors. As Paul threw a bundle of sticks on the fire, what fastened on his hand?
answer: A venomous snake driven out by the heat
choices: A venomous snake driven out by the heat
A spark that burned his palm to the bone
A scorpion he had not seen on the wood
A burning brand that no one could pull loose
context: Acts 27-28. The locals expected Paul to swell up and die - a clear sign of guilt - but he shook the snake into the fire and was unharmed. They then took him for a god. Paul stayed three months on Malta, healed the father of Publius the chief official, and won the gratitude of the islanders. He sailed on to Rome and lived two years there under house arrest awaiting trial, preaching freely to all who came.

question: On Paul's second missionary journey, a vision called him to cross from Asia Minor into Europe. He landed at Philippi, a Roman colony with no synagogue. On the Sabbath he went outside the city gate to the river, where he expected to find a Jewish prayer-meeting. He found a small group of women. One was a businesswoman from the city of Thyatira, a dealer in expensive cloth dyed with murex shellfish. She listened, was baptized with her whole household, and insisted Paul stay at her house. What was her trade?
answer: A seller of purple cloth
choices: A seller of purple cloth
A baker of festival bread
A weaver of linen sails
A merchant of olive oil
context: Acts 16:11-15. Her name was Lydia - likely a trade name ('a Lydian woman'). Tyrian purple was the most expensive dye in the ancient world, extracted from rotting murex sea snails, so a 'seller of purple' was wealthy. Lydia's house became the meeting-place of the first Christian church in Europe. The Philippian church remained Paul's favorite - the Letter to the Philippians is his warmest and most affectionate.

question: After being run out of the synagogue at Thessalonica by a mob, Paul and Silas slipped away by night to the city of Berea in what is now northern Greece. The Jews there received the new teaching very differently from the Thessalonians. Luke, the author of Acts, gives them an unusual compliment: 'These were more noble than those of Thessalonica.' What did the Bereans do that earned them the praise?
answer: Searched the Scriptures daily to check whether what Paul said was true
choices: Searched the Scriptures daily to check whether what Paul said was true
Welcomed Paul into the most prominent home in the city
Refused to listen until they had paid the temple tax
Fed Paul and Silas from the synagogue treasury
context: Acts 17:10-12. The Bereans became the proverbial model of independent-minded believers - willing to be taught but unwilling to take any teacher's word without checking. Many believed, including some prominent Greek women and men. The Thessalonian mob followed Paul to Berea and stirred up trouble again; Paul went on alone to Athens while Silas and Timothy stayed behind. The 'noble Bereans' became a stock phrase in Protestant rhetoric for testing every claim against the source.

question: An eloquent Jewish scholar from Alexandria named Apollos arrived in Ephesus, mighty in the Scriptures and burning with zeal - but he had only heard of the baptism of John, not the fuller story of Jesus. He began preaching boldly in the synagogue. A married couple in the congregation, tentmakers and old friends of Paul, took Apollos aside privately and explained the way of God more accurately. Then they sent him on with letters of recommendation to the brothers in Achaia. Who was the couple?
answer: Priscilla and Aquila
choices: Priscilla and Aquila
Ananias and Sapphira
Lazarus and Mary of Bethany
Crispus and Sosthenes
context: Acts 18:24-28. Priscilla and Aquila had been expelled from Rome by Emperor Claudius's 49 AD edict against Jews; they met Paul in Corinth, traveled with him to Ephesus, and worked alongside him at their shared trade of tentmaking. Their gentle correction of Apollos is one of the most-cited New Testament examples of teaching done privately and respectfully. Apollos became a major Christian leader; Paul mentions him several times in 1 Corinthians.

question: Early in his ministry, Jesus climbed a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, sat down (the rabbinic posture for teaching), and delivered the longest single block of his recorded teaching - three chapters in Matthew, two in Luke. The opening section is a series of paradoxical blessings, each beginning 'Blessed are...' - the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. By what name are these opening blessings collectively known?
answer: The Beatitudes
choices: The Beatitudes
The Antitheses
The Magnificat
The Benedictus
context: Matthew 5-7. The word 'beatitude' comes from the Latin 'beatus' ('blessed' or 'happy'), translating the Greek 'makarios'. The Sermon on the Mount also contains the Lord's Prayer, 'You are the salt of the earth, the light of the world,' the Golden Rule, the lilies of the field passage, the warning against judging others, and the parable of the wise and foolish builders. The crowds at the end were 'astonished, for he taught them as one having authority.'

question: In April 1429 the English had besieged the French city of Orleans for seven months and France stood on the brink of losing the Hundred Years' War. A 17-year-old peasant girl from Domremy named Joan, who said Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret had ordered her to save France, arrived in white armor with a banner. She led the troops at the fortress of Les Tourelles, was struck in the shoulder by an arrow, pulled it out herself, and went back into the fight. How long did the siege last after she came?
answer: Nine days; the English withdrew on May 8, 1429
choices: Nine days; the English withdrew on May 8, 1429
Six months; until the autumn harvest that year
One full year; until the next campaigning season
Two weeks; until reinforcements from Burgundy arrived
context: Joan went on to lead the French to victory at Patay (June 1429) and brought the Dauphin to Reims to be crowned King Charles VII (July 17, 1429) - the place where French kings had been crowned for centuries. She was captured at Compiegne in May 1430 by Burgundians who sold her to the English. Tried for heresy at Rouen by an ecclesiastical court, she was burned at the stake on May 30, 1431, age 19. She was canonized as a saint in 1920.

question: The young Augustine had spent years torn between his mother Monica's Christian faith and his own skeptical mind. In August 386 AD, in a Milan garden, he sat weeping under a fig tree, ashamed of his inability to leave his old life. He heard a child's voice from a neighboring house chanting over and over: 'Tolle lege' (Take and read). He took it as a sign, opened the book lying nearby (Paul's letter to the Romans), and read the first passage his eye fell on. What did he do next?
answer: Closed the book and resolved to be baptized that Easter
choices: Closed the book and resolved to be baptized that Easter
Burned all his books of pagan philosophy in the garden fire
Walked to his mother's house in tears to ask forgiveness
Ordered his slaves freed and gave his land to the poor
context: Augustine tells the story in book VIII of his Confessions (c. 397-400 AD), one of the first autobiographies in Western literature. The passage he read was Romans 13:13-14 - 'Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in debauchery and licentiousness... put on the Lord Jesus Christ.' He was baptized at the Easter Vigil 387 by Ambrose, bishop of Milan; his mother Monica died shortly after. Augustine returned to North Africa, became bishop of Hippo, and wrote The City of God and the Confessions.

question: Around 270 AD a young Egyptian named Anthony heard the words of Jesus 'If you would be perfect, go sell what you have and give to the poor,' and did exactly that. He gave away his inheritance, placed his sister in a convent, and walked alone into the Egyptian desert to live as a hermit in an abandoned Roman fort. He stayed there twenty years, eating bread brought twice a year. When his admirers eventually broke the door down expecting to find him dead or mad, in what condition did they find him?
answer: Calm, healthy, and full of dignity at age 55
choices: Calm, healthy, and full of dignity at age 55
Emaciated and blind from years without sunlight
Wandering and muttering in a tongue no one knew
Surrounded by the bones of the wild beasts he had killed
context: Anthony's biography was written by Athanasius (the same bishop who fought Arius at Nicaea) around 360 AD and became one of the most influential books in Western Christianity - Augustine in the Confessions cites it as one of the books that pushed him toward his own conversion. Anthony is considered the father of Christian monasticism. He lived to age 105, dying around 356 AD, and is depicted in art tormented by demons (Bosch and Grunewald painted famous Temptations of Saint Anthony).

question: According to medieval legend, Catherine of Alexandria was an 18-year-old princess of Alexandria who had memorized all of philosophy and theology and used her learning to argue down a panel of fifty pagan philosophers the emperor Maxentius had assembled to refute her - she converted them instead, and they were burned. Maxentius ordered her killed on a device of four spiked wheels designed to tear her body apart. What happened when she was bound to the wheel?
answer: The wheel shattered at her touch, killing onlookers with flying pieces
choices: The wheel shattered at her touch, killing onlookers with flying pieces
An angel descended and unbound her from the iron straps
A great storm extinguished every torch around the device
The spikes turned to soft wax against her bare skin
context: Catherine was finally beheaded. The 'Catherine wheel' is named after her - both the firework that spins on a frame and the medieval torture device. Her body was said to have been carried by angels to Mount Sinai, where the monastery of Saint Catherine (the oldest continually inhabited Christian monastery in the world, founded by the Emperor Justinian in 565 AD) still stands. Joan of Arc named Catherine as one of the saints whose voice told her to save France.

question: According to medieval Christian legend (the Golden Legend, 13th century), a dragon had made its lair beside the only spring of a city in Libya called Silene. To stop it from poisoning the water, the citizens gave it two sheep a day. When the sheep ran out, they cast lots for human victims. The lot eventually fell on the king's daughter, dressed as a bride and led out to the spring to be eaten. A young Christian soldier passing by, mounted on a white horse, fought and pinned the dragon to the ground with his lance. What was the soldier's name?
answer: George
choices: George
Michael
Theodore
Demetrius
context: George then offered to kill the dragon if the citizens would be baptized. Fifteen thousand were baptized on the spot. The historical George is much older than the dragon legend - a 3rd-century Roman soldier of Cappadocia, martyred under Diocletian around 303 AD by being dragged through the streets and beheaded. He became patron saint of England (Edward III put him on the flag of the Order of the Garter, 1348) and of soldiers, scouts, and many cities (Genoa, Moscow, Beirut, Georgia).

question: Sebastian was a high-ranking officer of the Praetorian Guard under the Roman Emperor Diocletian, a Christian in secret who used his position to encourage condemned believers and even convert other officers. When his faith was discovered around 287 AD, Diocletian ordered him tied to a stake in a field and shot full of arrows by his own Numidian archers. They left him for dead. A Christian widow named Irene came that night to bury him and discovered something. What?
answer: Sebastian was still alive; the arrows had not hit a vital organ
choices: Sebastian was still alive; the arrows had not hit a vital organ
His body had disappeared, leaving only blood on the stake
The arrows had reversed themselves and faced the archers
A great hound stood guard over his body in the dark
context: Irene nursed him back to health. Sebastian then deliberately confronted Diocletian on the steps of the imperial palace and denounced him for persecuting Christians. The emperor, stunned that Sebastian was alive, ordered him clubbed to death on the spot, his body thrown into the Roman sewer. Christians recovered the body and buried it in the catacombs that still bear his name. Sebastian is one of the most-painted saints in Western art - Mantegna, Botticelli, Perugino, El Greco, Reni, and many others.

question: In August 258 AD, Emperor Valerian ordered all Christian bishops, priests, and deacons executed. Pope Sixtus II was beheaded; his archdeacon Lawrence followed three days later. The Roman prefect demanded Lawrence hand over the treasures of the church within three days. On the day, Lawrence arrived leading a great procession - but instead of gold he brought the city's poor, blind, lame, and lepers, saying 'These are the true treasures of the church.' The infuriated prefect ordered an unusually slow execution. What was it?
answer: Roasted alive on an iron gridiron over coals
choices: Roasted alive on an iron gridiron over coals
Crucified upside-down at the city gate
Boiled in a copper cauldron of olive oil
Buried alive beneath a marble slab
context: Legend says that halfway through, Lawrence quipped to his torturers: 'You can turn me over now - I am cooked on this side.' He died praying for the conversion of Rome. Lawrence is one of the most popular saints of Rome; the church of San Lorenzo fuori le Mura stands over his tomb. His feast day (August 10) coincides with the Perseid meteor shower, popularly called 'the tears of Saint Lawrence.' The Escorial palace in Spain is built in the shape of his gridiron.

question: Around 1206 in Assisi, the 24-year-old Francesco Bernardone, son of the wealthy cloth merchant Pietro, had been giving away his father's money to rebuild a ruined chapel called San Damiano. His furious father dragged Francis before the bishop in the public square to demand the money back and disinherit him. Francis stripped off every piece of clothing he was wearing, folded it, laid it and a purse of money at his father's feet. What did he say next?
answer: Until now I called you father; now I say only 'Our Father in heaven'
choices: Until now I called you father; now I say only 'Our Father in heaven'
Forgive me, father, for I do not know what else I can do today
Take back your clothes and let me go in peace from this city
I will pay you double in a year, but the chapel must stand
context: The bishop covered Francis with his own cloak. Francis walked off naked toward the woods singing - the founding scene of the Franciscan order. He gathered companions, lived in evangelical poverty, preached to birds and reportedly tamed a wolf at Gubbio, and in 1224 on Mount La Verna received the stigmata - the wounds of Christ's crucifixion in his hands, feet, and side, the first recorded case in Christian history. He died at age 44 in 1226. Giotto's frescoes at Assisi tell the story.

question: Jesus, his mother Mary, and his disciples attended a wedding feast in the Galilean village of Cana when the wine ran out - a serious social disaster for the host family. Mary mentioned the problem to Jesus, who answered: 'Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.' Mary turned to the servants and said simply: 'Do whatever he tells you.' Jesus ordered six stone water jars filled to the brim and told the servants to draw some out for the master of the banquet. What did the master say after he tasted it?
answer: You have saved the best wine for last
choices: You have saved the best wine for last
This is fit for the high priest in Jerusalem
Where did you find this in the village so late
Even Galilee has no vineyard that grows such wine
context: John 2:1-11. The transformation produced about 150 gallons of fine wine - far more than the wedding party could ever drink. John calls this the first of the 'signs' in his Gospel; the other six signs (the official's son, the lame man at Bethesda, the feeding of the 5,000, walking on water, the man born blind, and Lazarus) build through John 11. The wedding at Cana is the source of the phrase 'his hour has not yet come' for the appointed moment of Jesus's death.

question: Near the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem was a pool with five covered porches called Bethesda. A great number of sick, blind, lame, and paralyzed people lay there, believing the water was occasionally stirred by an angel and that the first into the pool afterward was healed. Jesus saw one man among them who had been an invalid 38 years. Jesus asked him: 'Do you want to be healed?' The man answered that he had no one to put him in the water. Jesus did not put him in the water. What did Jesus tell him to do?
answer: Get up, take up your bed, and walk
choices: Get up, take up your bed, and walk
Wash your eyes and feet in the pool
Wait one more hour for the angel to come
Stand and lift your hands toward the temple
context: John 5:1-15. The man was healed at once and walked. It was the Sabbath; the religious authorities saw him carrying his bedroll and rebuked him for breaking Sabbath law. He pointed at Jesus. This was one of the early flashpoints between Jesus and the Jerusalem authorities. Archaeology located the Pool of Bethesda in the 19th century - exactly as John described, five porticoes, on the north side of the Temple Mount near the Church of Saint Anne.

question: Passing through Jericho on his way to Jerusalem for the final Passover, Jesus came upon a crowd lining the road. A short, wealthy chief tax collector named Zacchaeus could not see over the crowd. Tax collectors in Roman-occupied Judea were despised collaborators who skimmed from their countrymen. Determined to see Jesus, Zacchaeus ran ahead and climbed a tree. Jesus stopped under it, looked up, called him by name, and told him to come down. What did Zacchaeus announce on the spot?
answer: Half my goods to the poor; fourfold restitution to anyone I cheated
choices: Half my goods to the poor; fourfold restitution to anyone I cheated
I will sell every house I own and leave Jericho forever
All my taxes I refuse to collect from this day forward
I will fast every Sabbath for one year of penance
context: Luke 19:1-10. The sycamore tree (sycomore-fig, Ficus sycomorus) is short and easy to climb. The Mosaic law required a thief to repay fourfold (Exodus 22:1); Zacchaeus's voluntary fourfold restitution is the full legal restitution for theft, applied to himself. Jesus's reply - 'Today salvation has come to this house' - and his self-description in this scene, 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,' is one of the clearest statements of his mission in any Gospel.

question: About a week after foretelling his own coming death in Jerusalem, Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain alone to pray. While he was praying, his appearance changed: his face shone like the sun and his clothes became dazzlingly white. Two figures from the Hebrew Bible appeared and spoke with him. A voice from a bright cloud declared: 'This is my beloved Son with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.' Which two figures appeared with Jesus on the mountain?
answer: Moses and Elijah
choices: Moses and Elijah
Abraham and David
Isaiah and Jeremiah
Adam and Noah
context: Matthew 17, Mark 9, Luke 9. Moses represents the Law and Elijah the Prophets - the entire Old Testament tradition appearing alongside Jesus on the mount. Peter, dazed, proposed building three tabernacles. The mountain has traditionally been identified as Mount Tabor (Eastern Orthodox tradition) or Mount Hermon (some scholars). The Eastern Orthodox feast of the Transfiguration on August 6 is one of the great feasts of the Christian year.

question: In the last week of his life, Jesus walked into the outer courtyard of the Jerusalem Temple at Passover and found it filled with money-changers (who converted pilgrim coins into Tyrian shekels for the temple tax) and dealers selling sacrificial doves, sheep, and oxen at high markup. He fashioned a whip out of cords. He overturned the tables, scattered the coins, and drove out the animals. What did he shout, quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah?
answer: My house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers
choices: My house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers
Tear down this temple, and in three days I will rebuild it again
Woe to you who buy and sell within these holy and consecrated walls
The Lord himself drives the wicked from his holy and chosen place
context: Matthew 21, Mark 11, Luke 19, John 2 (with John placing it at the beginning of the ministry rather than the end). The Court of the Gentiles - where the merchants set up - was the only area of the Temple open to non-Jewish worshippers; Jesus's outrage was that the noise of commerce had made prayer impossible there. The action helped seal the resolve of the chief priests to have him killed before the Passover week was over.

question: After ten plagues broke Pharaoh's will, the Hebrews under Moses left Egypt with flocks and the bones of Joseph. Pharaoh pursued them with 600 chariots. The Hebrews, trapped against the Red Sea, panicked. Moses stretched out his staff; a strong east wind blew all night, driving back the waters and making the seabed dry. The Hebrews crossed; the Egyptian army followed in. As dawn came, Moses stretched out his hand again. What happened to the Egyptians?
answer: The waters returned and drowned them all; not one survived
choices: The waters returned and drowned them all; not one survived
A pillar of fire blocked their charge from above the seabed
Their horses bolted and trampled them in the deep mud below
A great wind blew the chariot wheels far apart in the night
context: Exodus 14. Miriam, sister of Moses, led the women with timbrels in a victory dance, singing 'Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea' (Exodus 15:21) - one of the oldest poetic fragments in the Bible. The Hebrew phrase 'yam suf' (literally 'sea of reeds') is the source of debate over whether the crossing was at the modern Red Sea or one of the shallower lakes to the north. The story is read by Jews at every Passover seder.

question: Moses had fled Egypt after killing an Egyptian overseer and lived forty years as a shepherd in Midian, married to Zipporah, daughter of the priest Jethro. Herding his father-in-law's flock near Mount Horeb one day, he saw a bush burning but not consumed by the fire. He turned aside to look. A voice from the bush ordered him to take off his sandals (the ground was holy) and commissioned him to lead the Hebrews to freedom. When Moses asked what name to give the Hebrews, what did the voice answer?
answer: I AM WHO I AM; tell them I AM has sent you
choices: I AM WHO I AM; tell them I AM has sent you
The Lord of Heaven, who made the stars and the sea
The God of fire, who has chosen Israel from all nations
The Mighty One, who breaks the bow of the proud forever
context: Exodus 3. The Hebrew is 'Ehyeh asher ehyeh' - the divine name from which the four-letter YHWH (the Tetragrammaton) was derived, traditionally rendered as 'the Lord' in most English Bibles because Jews after the exile stopped pronouncing it aloud. Moses tried to refuse the call five times (he was slow of speech, the people would not believe him, etc.); God finally allowed his brother Aaron to be his spokesman. Moses returned to Egypt at age eighty.

question: Through Moses and Aaron, God sent nine plagues on Pharaoh: the Nile to blood, frogs, gnats, flies, livestock disease, boils, hail with fire, locusts, three days of darkness. Pharaoh still refused. For the tenth and final plague, God ordered every Hebrew household to slaughter a year-old lamb and paint the blood on the doorposts and lintel. At midnight a destroying angel passed through Egypt, and over the marked Hebrew houses. What did the angel do?
answer: Killed every firstborn of humans and livestock in unmarked houses
choices: Killed every firstborn of humans and livestock in unmarked houses
Set every Egyptian palace on fire from the inside out
Struck every Egyptian temple priest blind for one year
Carried away all the cattle and chariots of Egypt by force
context: Exodus 11-12. Pharaoh's own firstborn son was killed that night. He summoned Moses before dawn and ordered the Hebrews to leave at once. The Jewish festival of Passover ('Pesach,' 'passing over') commemorates the angel's passing over the blood-marked houses; the Christian Holy Week takes its shape from the same week - Jesus called himself the Passover Lamb whose blood marks the door. The Hebrews left in such haste their bread had no time to rise, the origin of unleavened bread (matzah).

question: During the forty years in the wilderness, the Hebrews complained against Moses about the manna ('worthless food') and the lack of water. God sent venomous snakes ('fiery serpents') into the camp and many died of snake-bite. The people repented and begged Moses to ask God to take the snakes away. God instructed Moses to do something specific, and any snake-bitten person who looked at it would live. What did Moses make?
answer: A bronze serpent and mounted it on a tall pole
choices: A bronze serpent and mounted it on a tall pole
A great heap of stones in the center of the camp
A circle of seven altars facing the rising sun
A wooden ark covered in beaten silver scales
context: Numbers 21:4-9. The bronze serpent ('Nehushtan' in Hebrew) survived into the time of King Hezekiah, who destroyed it 700 years later because Israelites had begun burning incense to it as an idol (2 Kings 18:4). Jesus referenced the story in John 3:14 - 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up' - making the bronze serpent a traditional Christian type of the crucifixion. The caduceus and the rod of Asclepius in medical symbols both echo the same image.

question: When famine struck Israel, Naomi and her husband Elimelech moved with their two sons to Moab. The sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, but within ten years all three men had died, leaving three widows. Naomi decided to return to Bethlehem and told her daughters-in-law to go back to their own mothers. Orpah kissed Naomi and turned back. Ruth refused. Her famous reply has been a model of loyal commitment for three thousand years. What did Ruth say?
answer: Where you go I will go; your people my people, your God my God
choices: Where you go I will go; your people my people, your God my God
Leave me not, mother, the road is long and the wolves are near
I am your daughter; my dead husband would weep to see me leave
I will return to Moab only if you forbid me with your hand
context: Ruth 1. Ruth followed Naomi to Bethlehem and gleaned grain from the fields of a wealthy kinsman named Boaz, who eventually married her under the levirate redemption law. Their great-grandson was King David - making Ruth the Moabite a great-great-grandmother of David and an ancestress of Jesus (Matthew lists her in the genealogy at Matthew 1:5). The Book of Ruth is one of only two books of the Hebrew Bible named after a woman (the other is Esther).

question: Elijah and his disciple Elisha walked together toward the Jordan River. Elijah rolled up his cloak, struck the water, and the river parted; they crossed on dry ground. Elijah asked Elisha what he could do for him before he was taken away. Elisha asked for a double portion of Elijah's prophetic spirit. Elijah answered: 'You have asked a hard thing. But if you see me when I am taken from you, it shall be granted.' What happened as they walked?
answer: A chariot and horses of fire separated them; Elijah rose to heaven in a whirlwind
choices: A chariot and horses of fire separated them; Elijah rose to heaven in a whirlwind
A great cloud descended and lifted Elijah into the sky alone
Elijah collapsed and was buried by angels in an unknown grave
Elijah walked into the Jordan and was carried away by the current
context: 2 Kings 2. Elijah's cloak fell behind him; Elisha picked it up, struck the river with it, and crossed back the same way, inheriting the prophetic office. Elijah is one of only two figures in the Hebrew Bible who never died (the other is Enoch, Genesis 5:24). Jewish tradition holds Elijah will return to announce the Messiah - a chair and a cup are still set for him at the Passover seder. He appeared with Moses on the Mount of Transfiguration.

question: In the Galilean village of Nazareth, a young woman named Mary, engaged to a carpenter named Joseph, was visited by the angel Gabriel. He greeted her: 'Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you.' Mary was deeply troubled. Gabriel told her she would conceive and bear a son and name him Jesus, and that he would rule on the throne of David forever. Mary asked the practical question: how, since she was a virgin? Gabriel answered. What did Mary then say?
answer: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word
choices: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word
How can a sword pass through me who has known no man at all
Bring word to my mother that I may speak with her first now
Tell Joseph what you have spoken before he sends me away from him
context: Luke 1:26-38. Gabriel told her that her cousin Elizabeth (long thought barren) was already six months pregnant. Mary went to visit Elizabeth in the hill country of Judea; Elizabeth's unborn child (John the Baptist) leaped in her womb in recognition. Mary then sang the Magnificat ('My soul magnifies the Lord...'), one of the great poetic moments of the Gospels. The Annunciation traditionally occurred on March 25 - exactly nine months before Christmas.

question: Sometime after Jesus's birth in Bethlehem, magi from the East (astrologer-priests of Persian tradition) arrived in Jerusalem asking where the new 'king of the Jews' had been born; they had followed his star. King Herod the Great, deeply troubled, summoned his own scribes, who quoted Micah 5:2: the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem. Herod sent the magi on with instructions to report back so he too could go and worship. The star led them to a house in Bethlehem. They opened their treasures and presented three gifts. What were the three gifts?
answer: Gold, frankincense, and myrrh
choices: Gold, frankincense, and myrrh
Silver, cedar oil, and saffron
A crown, a scepter, and a purple robe
Wheat, wine, and a lamb without blemish
context: Matthew 2:1-12. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, the magi went home by another way. Herod, learning he had been outwitted, ordered the murder of every male child in Bethlehem under age two (the Massacre of the Innocents). Joseph fled with Mary and Jesus to Egypt, returning only after Herod's death. The traditional names Caspar, Melchior, and Balthasar are later additions; Matthew does not say there were three magi, only three gifts. Gold for a king; frankincense for a priest; myrrh (used to embalm) foreshadowing his death.
